clue.text: Implying that there must be a point somewhere…

definitions.text: Implying that there must be a point somewhere…

parts.words: Implying that there must be a point somewhere
parts.note: read literally, something central that everything turns on must have a fixed point around which it swings

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a remark about a pointless discussion; the cryptic reading is the literal turning point of a hinge or lever.
explanation.definitionFit: Something crucial is the turning point of a matter, the spot on which everything hinges.

clue.text: There was no evidence of its use burial of Sir John Moore.

definitions.text: There was no evidence of its use burial of Sir John Moore.

parts.words: There was no evidence of its use burial of Sir John Moore
parts.note: alludes to the poem The Burial of Sir John Moore after Corunna, which opens 'Not a drum was heard, not a funeral note'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held seems to have lost 'at the' before 'burial'. Charles Wolfe's poem says no drum was heard, so the beater of one was never used.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer strikes the skin with this wooden beater, which would sound at a military funeral.

clue.text: Friday certainly wasn't pay-day

parts.note: Man Friday was the unpaid servant of the castaway in Defoe's novel, so for his master Friday cost nothing

explanation.walkthrough: Friday looks like the weekday when wages are handed out; it is the companion in Daniel Defoe's 1719 desert-island novel, who was never paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's shipwrecked hero took the islander Friday as his servant without any wages.

clue.text: Getting on with the argument hastening publication.

explanation.surface: Someone pressing a debate to a conclusion while rushing a book out.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing a dispute to a decision is the idiom; read literally, it means rushing out an edition of a magazine.

clue.text: He raises his voice suddenly to wrong doer yell.

indicators.note: putting the letters of these two words wrong means jumbling them into a new order

explanation.surface: A man's sudden shout at a villain who has wronged him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges the letters of DOER and YELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpine singing jumps abruptly from chest voice into falsetto and back.

definitions.text: Prepare to go on the journey

indicators.note: the letters sit in the run of the words that follow, across the gap between them

explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters inside 'decENT RAINcoat'.
explanation.definitionFit: To board a train is to get ready for a rail journey.

clue.text: Strong points about uncertainties.

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning

explanation.surface: An argument whose strengths concern its doubtful areas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong points' sounds like the merits of an argument; it means small military forts.
explanation.definitionFit: These are fortified outworks, places built to be held strongly against attack.

clue.text: The weasel's serenade? It's on anyway.

definitions.text: The weasel's serenade? It's on anyway.

parts.words: The weasel's serenade? It's on anyway
parts.note: the nursery song says 'pop goes the weasel', so the weasel's tune is a pop one, and chart songs are playing everywhere

explanation.walkthrough: The old rhyme 'Pop Goes the Weasel' supplies the first word; the second half suggests it is always on the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Chart songs aimed at a wide audience are called popular, shortened to pop.

clue.text: A sheltered path to be made up, drift?

parts.note: the lee is the side protected from the wind
a way is a road or path

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a sheltered path that has yet to be built.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship blown sideways off course has distance to recover, which sailors call making it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Sideways drift of a vessel downwind is the nautical sense, hence lost ground still to be recovered.

clue.text: Sort of light dwelling place in the East End.

parts.note: limelight was the old stage lighting, so lime is a sort of light

explanation.surface: A kind of lamp found in a London home.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the traditionally working-class district of east London by the docks; this area lies beside the Thames there.
explanation.definitionFit: This district of Tower Hamlets lies in London's East End beside the river.

clue.text: Made an exchange of practical skill in a mixed breed.

indicators.note: the skill word is placed in the jumbled breed
a mixed breed is a crossbreed, so the letters of the word breed are mixed up

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of cooking

explanation.surface: Swapping a mongrel dog for some useful know-how.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' turns BREED into B...ERED, and 'in' puts ART inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade goods without money is to swap them, which is to make an exchange.

clue.text: A looseness in the machinery of punishment?

definitions.text: A looseness in the machinery of punishment?

parts.words: A looseness in the machinery of punishment
parts.note: play between parts of a mechanism, read again as a whipping given across the back

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as slackness in a penal system; the technical sense is slack in gears, and literally it is a flogging stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Engineers call the play between meshing gears by this term; a stroke of the whip on the shoulders would also fit.

clue.text: Have a go at it, anyhow — the play's exciting.

indicators.note: anyhow means haphazardly, so the letters are thrown together in any order

explanation.surface: An urge to have a try at something because a drama is thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' jumbles A GO AT IT. 'Play' is musical playing, not a stage drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction asks performers to play in an agitated, excited manner.

clue.text: Palindromic pick-mc-up.

indicators.note: the word wanted reads the same from either end, which is all the wordplay offers

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.walkthrough: 'Palindromic' tells you only that the word for a tonic reads identically backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic or stimulating drink that restores your spirits is a restorative.

clue.text: "Thou wilt not with Predestination round me" (Omar Khayyam).

definitions.text: "Thou wilt not with Predestination round me" (Omar Khayyam).

parts.words: Thou wilt not with Predestination round me
parts.note: a line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam with its verb missing; the solver supplies the word for trapping in a net

explanation.walkthrough: FitzGerald's line runs 'Thou wilt not with Predestined Evil round / Enmesh, and then impute my Fall to Sin'; the gap is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to catch as in a net, to entangle.

parts.note: a bagpipe player often performs a lament, a mournful tune, so his music is literally lament-able

explanation.walkthrough: 'lamentable' seems to mean that he plays badly; a lament is a Scottish funeral tune for the pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagpipe musicians traditionally play laments at funerals.

clue.text: "Observe how into other planets circle other suns."

definitions.text: "Observe how into other planets circle other suns."

parts.words: Observe how into other planets circle other suns
parts.note: lines from Pope's Essay on Man with a word gapped; the solver supplies the missing noun for an organised set of bodies

explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means an ordered arrangement of bodies, like planets round a star.
